why: The four options are every price tested: €0.08 is what you get if you ignore stationery or forget to weight by customers, €0.06 maximises volume and €0.09 the margin per page; the slips that still land on €0.07 (taking the €3 as profit, or using the industry's 10% margin) are the two sourceHas names.

6 points uses the 'considered buying' row (46.3% vs 40.5%), 2 points uses the 'used now or in the past' or 'use now' row (about 1.9 or 2.1 points), and 31 is the gap taken as a relative percent on the one-person base (21.8 / 71.2 = 30.6%); each is a slip.
Homes over 30% (actually 27.4%) and public buildings over 5% (4.6%) are near-miss figures, and 43% for buildings comes from leaving public buildings out (8.4 / 19.7 = 42.6%); all are fair.

+$22,000 reverses the sign, -$40,000 forgets the 10% volume rise and applies $4.20 to every bag (200k x 10c = $20k against $60k), and +$40,000 ignores both the price tier and the $1.70 handling cost (220k x $2 against 200k x $2); each takes one or two slips.

58% is a near miss for the true 56.6%, Inventory beating Timesheets is a careless reading of two equal $0.40m ratios, and 'most profitable' is the one statement the data does not cover, which sourceHas lists.

DentaCare making more profit reads its higher margin as higher profit, and Brightway spending more on premises reads a percentage as an amount (both over-readings); the check-up price is the one statement the data does not cover, which sourceHas lists.

50% is a near miss for the true 48.3%, Word puzzles beating Farming is a careless reading of two equal $0.50m ratios, and 'most profitable' is the one statement the data does not cover, which sourceHas lists.

Washwell making more profit reads its higher margin as higher profit, and Crestline spending more on vans reads a percentage as an amount (both over-readings); price per item is the one statement the data does not cover, which sourceHas lists.

The 2% sales rise catches anyone who forgets that fuel costs rise with sales ($7.6m looks bigger than $7.1m), the 2% operating-cost cut takes the percent without its much smaller base, and the tanker-fleet option is ruled out by the operating-cost option alone, which sourceHas lists.

Half compares 2016 revenues and forgets the margins (0.54), twice compares margins alone (11/6 = 1.83), and three times is the coarse filler sourceHas lists; skipping the growth step still lands on 'the same', which sourceHas names as a slip that does so in the source too.
